🧠 Overview Start here

This resource covers the two lectures on Spinal Tracts — spinal cord gray/white matter topography, the ascending (sensory) pathways, the descending (motor) pathways, and their clinical correlations — delivered by Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen as part of the CNS Neurology course.

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the gray and white matter topography of the spinal cord in cross-section
  • Trace the three-neuron chain of the posterior column–medial lemniscus pathway
  • Trace the anterior and lateral spinothalamic tracts and their somatotopic organization
  • Trace the posterior, anterior, and cuneocerebellar spinocerebellar pathways
  • Identify the major descending motor tracts and their functional roles
  • Apply spinal-tract anatomy to localize lesions (spastic vs. flaccid paralysis)

🗺️ Lecture Roadmap

  • Part 1 — Gray/white matter topography, Rexed laminae, ascending tract anatomy (posterior column, spinothalamic, spinocerebellar), descending tract anatomy
  • Part 2 — Clinical application: spastic vs. flaccid limbs, plexus lesions, and localization logic

📖 Key Definitions

  • Ascending tract — carries sensory information upward, toward the brain
  • Descending tract — carries motor commands downward, toward the periphery
  • Decussation — crossing of fibers to the opposite (contralateral) side
  • Somatotopic organization — orderly body-map arrangement of fibers within a tract
Why this lecture matters: Spinal tract anatomy is the anatomical backbone of the entire neurological examination. Every sensory and motor exam finding is interpreted by reasoning back through these pathways — this is one of the highest-yield topics in clinical neurology.

🧬 Spinal Cord Topography Foundations

Before learning individual tracts, the lecture establishes the internal map of the cord in axial (transverse) section — this map is the scaffold onto which every tract is placed.

Gray Matter — the "Butterfly" / "H" Shape

In axial cuts, the spinal cord's gray matter forms an H-shaped (butterfly-shaped) core, sitting centrally, surrounded laterally by white matter.

  • Gray matter is subdivided into a posterior (dorsal) horn, an anterior (ventral) horn, and — at thoracolumbar levels (T1–L2) only — a lateral horn.
  • The gray matter is further parcellated into 10 Rexed laminae (I–X), named for the anatomist who described this laminar organization.
  • Lamina II corresponds to the substantia gelatinosa; laminae IV–VI form the nucleus proprius; lamina VII contains the intermediolateral cell column; lamina IX contains motor neuron cell bodies in the anterior horn.
  • The same functional lamina can carry a different regional name depending on spinal level — e.g., what corresponds to lamina VII in the lumbar cord is named differently in the thoracic cord (this is the posterior thoracic nucleus / nucleus of Clarke, discussed under the spinocerebellar tracts).
  • Just lateral to lamina I lies the posterolateral tract of Lissauer, a discrete zone of thinly myelinated fibers, named after a German neurologist.

White Matter — Three Funiculi

White matter surrounding the gray matter is divided by the gray matter itself into three columns (funiculi) on each side:

Posterior funiculus

Lies between the two posterior horns.

Lateral funiculus

Lies between the posterior and anterior horns on each side. Most tractology of clinical interest is carried here.

Anterior funiculus

Lies between the two anterior horns.

High-yield: The lecturer stresses that the lateral funiculus is where the majority of ascending and descending tracts of clinical significance are located — keep this column in mind as the "traffic corridor" of the cord.

Anterior White Commissure

The anterior white commissure connects the two anterior funiculi across the midline. It can be described three equivalent ways:

  • The white-matter bridge between the two anterior funiculi
  • The structure lying posterior to the anterior median fissure
  • The structure lying anterior to the horizontal part of the gray matter (i.e., anterior to the central canal)

Its clinical importance: most ascending sensory pathways decussate here — fibers entering on the left cross to the right and vice versa, so a large share of tract crossing occurs at this exact site.

🖼️ Illustration — why decussation matters clinically
Because ascending pathways cross before reaching the cortex, damage above the crossing point (e.g., in the cerebral hemisphere) produces sensory or motor loss on the opposite side of the body.
Figure 6.5 — Topography of the spinal cord in transverse section: horns, sulci, funiculi, and Rexed laminae. The lateral horn is present only at thoracolumbar levels (T1–L2); the posterior intermediate sulcus/septum is present only above T6.
Topographic (somatotopic) organization of ascending pathways entering the dorsal columns, alongside the labeled cross-section of the cord showing motor and sensory pathway locations and Rexed lamina groupings.
Close-up cross-section: dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis/cuneatus), spinocerebellar tracts, spinothalamic tracts, and the descending motor pathways (corticospinal, rubrospinal, tectospinal/vestibulospinal/reticulospinal).

Somatotopic Organization — the Posterior Column Exception

The posterior column (dorsal column) is organized somatotopically in a specific order, from medial to lateral: Sacral → Lumbar → Thoracic → Cervical (sacral fibers are most medial; cervical fibers are most lateral).

High-yield — reversed pattern: This ordering is the opposite of most other ascending tracts. In the spinothalamic and spinocerebellar systems, sacral fibers tend to sit most laterally, and cervical fibers most medially. The posterior column is the exception.

Why the sacral (lower limb) fibers are placed most medially: the posterior column is heavily concerned with gait and balance — the body protects its most vital ascending fibers by tucking them deepest/most medially. The lecturer's example: the very act of sitting upright and maintaining posture right now is being interpreted through this pathway.

⬆️ I. Ascending Tracts Sensory

Ascending tracts represent functional pathways that convey sensory information from the periphery to higher levels. Almost all of them share a common organizational logic before their individual routes diverge.

Shared Features of Ascending Tracts

  • Usually built from a chain of three neurons: first-, second-, and third-order.
  • The first-order neuron is always located in the spinal (dorsal root) ganglion, regardless of tract or spinal level.
  • Most tracts decussate (cross to the contralateral side) before reaching their final destination.
  • Collateral branches from these neurons feed local spinal reflex arcs — for example, the instantaneous limb-withdrawal reflex to a painful stimulus, which occurs at the level of the cord itself, without waiting for cortical interpretation.
    • 🖼️ Illustration — the generic 3-neuron relay
    Generic three-neuron relay pattern shared by most ascending tracts (exact decussation site differs by tract — see each pathway's table above).
    Teaching analogy (first-order neuron): Think of the first-order neuron as a local bus station or port — all incoming "passengers" (impulses) from the periphery gather there first, then "board a connecting service" to the next relay station (the second-order neuron). Just as intercity buses often cross from one side of the road to the other at a specific junction en route, most ascending fibers cross to the opposite side at a specific decussation point before continuing to their destination.

    A. Posterior Column–Medial Lemniscus Pathway Uncrossed until medulla

    ▶

    Function: fine (discriminative) touch, conscious proprioception, and vibratory sense. Somatotopically organized (sacral most medial, as above).

    Receptors: Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner's corpuscles, joint receptors, muscle spindles, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs).

    OrderLocationCourse
    1st-orderSpinal ganglia, all levelsLower-extremity fibers form fasciculus gracilis (medial); upper-extremity fibers form fasciculus cuneatus (lateral). Axons ascend in the posterior columns and terminate in the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the caudal medulla.
    2nd-orderGracile & cuneate nuclei, caudal medullaAxons form the internal arcuate fibers, which decussate and form a compact bundle — the medial lemniscus — which ascends through the contralateral brainstem to the VPL nucleus of the thalamus.
    3rd-orderVPL nucleus of thalamusProjects via the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex, areas 3, 1, 2).
    "G is for Guwa" (inside/medial): Fasciculus Gracilis = lower limb, most medial. Fasciculus cuneatus = upper limb, lateral to gracilis.
    Decussation site: occurs in the medulla, via the internal arcuate fibers, just anterior to the central canal — the same general region shown earlier as the decussation point in the diagrams.
    Figure 7.5 — Schematic diagram of the major ascending and descending pathways of the spinal cord, shown at a single cross-sectional level.
    Figure 7.1 — The posterior column–medial lemniscus pathway, traced from peripheral receptor through the gracile/cuneate nuclei, decussation as internal arcuate fibers, medial lemniscus, VPL of thalamus, to the postcentral gyrus. Note the inverted (upside-down) body map at the cortex: lower-limb representation lies superomedially, upper-limb representation lies inferolaterally.
    Clinical correlation — cortical homunculus is inverted: at the postcentral gyrus, the lower limb is represented superiorly/medially and the upper limb inferiorly/laterally — because the right hemisphere controls the left body and vice versa, plus this vertical inversion, a strictly midline blow to the top of the head can selectively affect the lower limbs, while a lateral blow above the ear can selectively affect the upper limbs.
    🖼️ Illustration — the inverted body map
    Schematic (not to scale) of the sensory homunculus: the leg is represented near the vertex/midline, the arm more laterally and inferiorly — the same inversion applies to the motor precentral gyrus.

    B. Anterolateral System Crossed

    ▶

    1. Anterior Spinothalamic Tract

    Function: crude touch — the sensation produced by stroking glabrous skin with a wisp of cotton. Input from free nerve endings and Merkel tactile disks.

    OrderLocationCourse
    1st-orderSpinal ganglia, all levelsAxons enter via the medial root entry zone to second-order neurons in the posterior horn.
    2nd-orderPosterior hornAxons decussate in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the contralateral anterior funiculus.
    3rd-orderVPL nucleus of thalamusVia the posterior limb of the internal capsule and corona radiata to the postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2).

    2. Lateral Spinothalamic Tract

    Function: itch, pain, and temperature. Input from free nerve endings and thermal receptors, carried by A-δ (fast) and C (slow) pain fibers.

    Somatotopic organization: sacral fibers posterolaterally, cervical fibers anteromedially — matching the general "sacral-lateral" pattern of the anterolateral system (the reverse of the posterior column).

    OrderLocationCourse
    1st-orderSpinal ganglia, all levelsAxons project via the posterolateral tract of Lissauer to second-order neurons in the posterior horn.
    2nd-orderPosterior hornAxons decussate in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the anterior half of the lateral funiculus; give off collaterals to the reticular formation.
    3rd-orderVPL nucleus (and bilaterally in intralaminar nuclei)VPL neurons project via the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2). Intralaminar neurons project to the caudatoputamen and to the frontal/parietal cortex.
    Ascending pathways (left): posterior columns, lateral spinothalamic, anterior spinothalamic — each with sacral/lumbar/thoracic/cervical somatotopy. Descending pathways (right): lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts.
    Classic labeled cross-section showing the posterolateral tract (of Lissauer) immediately lateral to Rexed lamina I, alongside the dorsal/ventral spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, and descending motor fasciculi.
    Figure 7.2 — The lateral spinothalamic tract, traced from a free nerve ending through the first-order neuron in the spinal ganglion, second-order neuron in the posterior horn, decussation in the anterior white commissure, ascent through medulla/pons/midbrain as part of the spinothalamic system, to the third-order neuron in the VPL and its projection to the postcentral gyrus.
    Rexed laminae (I–X) on the left; corresponding named nuclei on the right — substantia gelatinosa (lamina II), nucleus proprius, dorsal nucleus/posterior thoracic nucleus (of Clarke), intermediolateral nucleus, and anterior horn motor neurons.

    C. Cerebellar (Spinocerebellar) Tracts Unconscious proprioception

    ▶

    These tracts sit most laterally within the lateral funiculus and carry unconscious proprioceptive information — as opposed to the posterior column's conscious proprioception.

    1. Posterior (Dorsal) Spinocerebellar Tract Uncrossed

    Transmits unconscious proprioceptive information for fine coordination of posture and movement of individual lower-limb muscles. Input from muscle spindles, GTOs, and pressure receptors.

    OrderLocationCourse
    1st-orderSpinal ganglia, C8–S3Axons enter via the medial root entry zone and synapse in the posterior thoracic nucleus (of Clarke).
    2nd-orderPosterior thoracic nucleus (C8–L3)Axons ascend in the lateral funiculus and reach the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, terminating ipsilaterally as mossy fibers in the rostral/caudal cerebellar vermis.

    2. Anterior (Ventral) Spinocerebellar Tract Crossed

    Concerned with coordinated movement and posture of the entire lower extremity. Same receptor inputs as above.

    OrderLocationCourse
    1st-orderSpinal ganglia, L1–S2Synapse on spinal border cells.
    2nd-orderSpinal border cells, anterior horns (L1–S2)Axons decussate in the anterior white commissure, ascend lateral to the lateral spinothalamic tract in the lateral funiculus, and enter the cerebellum via the superior cerebellar peduncle, terminating contralaterally as mossy fibers in the rostral cerebellar vermis.

    3. Cuneocerebellar Tract Uncrossed

    The upper-extremity equivalent of the posterior spinocerebellar tract.

    OrderLocationCourse
    1st-orderSpinal ganglia, C2–T7Axons travel via the fasciculus cuneatus to the caudal medulla and synapse in the accessory cuneate nucleus (a homolog of the posterior thoracic nucleus).
    2nd-orderAccessory cuneate nucleus, medullaAxons project ipsilaterally to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
    Figure 7.3 — Schematic of the anterior and posterior spinocerebellar tracts and the cuneocerebellar tract, from neuromuscular spindle/Golgi tendon organ receptors through the posterior thoracic nucleus and accessory cuneate nucleus to the cerebellar vermis.
    Unconscious muscle/joint sense pathways to the cerebellum: posterior spinocerebellar tract entering via the inferior cerebellar peduncle, anterior spinocerebellar tract entering via the superior cerebellar peduncle, relayed through the nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's column).

    ⬇️ II. Descending Tracts Motor

    Descending tracts are concerned with somatic and visceral motor activities. Their cells of origin lie either in the cerebral cortex (corticospinal tracts) or in the brainstem (rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal).

    A. Lateral Corticospinal (Pyramidal) Tract 90% crossed

    • Not fully myelinated until the end of the second year of life.
    • Concerned with volitional, skilled motor activity, primarily of the digits of the upper limb.
    • Receives input from the paracentral lobule (medial continuation of the motor/sensory cortices), which subserves the contralateral leg and foot muscles.
    • Arises from lamina V of the cerebral cortex, from three cortical areas: premotor cortex (area 6), precentral motor cortex (area 4), and postcentral sensory cortex (areas 3, 1, 2).
    • The axons of the giant cells of Betz contribute the largest-diameter fibers of the tract.
    • Course: posterior limb of the internal capsule → middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri of the midbrain → base of the pons → forms the pyramid of the medulla.
    • Undergoes 90% decussation at the caudal medulla (pyramidal decussation); the crossed fibers descend as the lateral corticospinal tract in the posterior quadrant of the lateral funiculus.
    • Terminates via interneurons on anterior horn motor neurons and posterior horn sensory neurons.
    High-yield: Transection of the lateral corticospinal tract results in spastic hemiparesis with a positive Babinski sign.

    B. Anterior Corticospinal Tract Uncrossed (until cord level)

    A small, largely uncrossed tract representing the remaining ~10% of corticospinal fibers that did not decussate at the medulla — instead they decussate at spinal cord levels in the anterior white commissure, close to the level where they synapse. Concerned with control of axial muscles.

    Section divider slide: Descending Tracts — corticospinal (lateral & anterior), rubrospinal, vestibulospinal.
    Figure 7.4 — The lateral and anterior corticospinal (pyramidal) tracts, from the giant pyramidal cells of Betz in the precentral gyrus, through the internal capsule, crus cerebri, basilar pons, medullary pyramid, pyramidal decussation, to motor end plates.

    C. Rubrospinal Tract Crossed

    • Arises in the contralateral red nucleus of the midbrain.
    • Plays a role in the control of flexor tone.
    • Lies anterior to the lateral corticospinal tract in the lateral funiculus.

    D. Vestibulospinal Tract Uncrossed

    • Arises from the giant cells of Deiters in the ipsilateral lateral vestibular nucleus.
    • Plays a role in the control of extensor tone.
    • Located in the anterior funiculus.

    Reticulospinal Tracts

    Arise from the reticular formation. Named by their brainstem origin:

    • Medullary reticulospinal tract — arises from the medulla oblongata.
    • Pontine reticulospinal tract — arises from the pons.

    Tectospinal Tract

    Arises from the tectum, the roof (most dorsal) part of the midbrain. Runs from the tectum down to the spinal cord.

    🩺 Clinical Correlations Second lecture

    The second lecture applies spinal-tract anatomy directly to the bedside question: why does one limb become spastic while another becomes flaccid after injury?

    The Two Inputs to Every Limb

    Each limb's motor output is driven by two converging sources of impulses:

    • The plexus itself (brachial plexus → upper limb; lumbosacral plexus → lower limb), which generates its own strong intrinsic motor signal.
    • Descending impulses from the cerebral cortex (via the corticospinal tract), which regulate and "smooth" that intrinsic signal into fine, controlled movement.
    🖼️ Illustration — tracing the two inputs to a limb
    Two independent inputs converge on every limb. A lesion above the plexus removes cortical regulation only (spastic); a lesion at the plexus itself removes the source signal entirely (flaccid).
    The lecturer's "generator" analogy: The local plexus is like a home generator — it can produce electricity on its own, but it runs uninhibited and "rough" unless regulated. The cortex is like the city power grid — it doesn't generate the raw power, but it regulates and stabilizes it. If the city grid fails but the local generator/house wiring is intact (a lesion above the plexus), the generator keeps firing on its own, unregulated → spasticity. If the generator/house wiring itself is destroyed (a lesion at or below the plexus), there is no power source left at all → flaccidity.
    Lesion siteWhat is lostResulting limb tone
    Cervical spine, above the brachial plexus (e.g., high neck trauma)Cortical regulation only — the brachial plexus itself is intact and keeps firingSpastic upper limb
    Brachial plexus itself (e.g., roots C5–T1 directly injured)Both the cortical input and the local plexus generatorFlaccid upper limb
    Spinal cord above the lumbosacral plexus (e.g., seat-belt fracture)Cortical regulation only — the lumbosacral plexus keeps firing unregulatedSpastic lower limb
    Lumbosacral plexus itself (e.g., gunshot wound directly to the plexus)Both the cortical input and the local plexus generatorFlaccid lower limb
    Bedside rule (UMN vs. LMN): A neck injury high above the brachial plexus → expect spastic upper limbs (loss of cortical regulation only). A seat-belt fracture damaging the cord above the lumbosacral plexus → expect spastic lower limbs. Direct plexus trauma (e.g., gunshot wound) that destroys the plexus itself → always flaccid, because the local "generator" of the impulse is destroyed.

    Spinal Reflex Arc

    When a painful stimulus contacts the skin (a hot surface, a snake, a sharp object), the sensation triggers an immediate motor withdrawal response at the level of the spinal cord itself — the limb is pulled away before conscious interpretation by the brain occurs. To the spinal reflex arc, the identity of the stimulus is irrelevant; only the painful sensation matters.

    Head Trauma Localization

    • A blow strictly to the top midline of the head can cause lower-limb deficits — the lower-limb cortical representation sits superiorly/medially.
    • A lateral blow above the ear can affect the upper limbs — their cortical representation sits inferiorly/laterally.

    Contralateral Deficits — Why the Side Matters

    Because of the medullary decussation of the posterior column–medial lemniscus pathway (and the earlier decussation of the spinothalamic tracts), a lesion in the cerebral cortex — or anywhere above the level of decussation — produces sensory/motor deficits on the opposite (contralateral) side of the body.

    🚨 High-Yield Exam Zone ⭐⭐⭐ Must know

    Exam Pearls

    The medial-to-lateral organization of the posterior column: Sacral (most medial) → Lumbar → Thoracic → Cervical (most lateral) — the opposite of most other spinal tracts.
    All ascending sensory pathways generally decussate. In the posterior column–medial lemniscus pathway, decussation occurs in the medulla via the internal arcuate fibers.
    The thalamic relay center for the major sensory pathways is the VPL (Ventral Posterior Lateral) nucleus. Mnemonic: THalamus is next to the THird ventricle.
    The pre-central gyrus (frontal lobe) governs motor function; the post-central gyrus (parietal lobe) governs sensory function.
    Cortical (and posterior-column) somatotopy is inverted: lower limb representation is superior/medial; upper limb representation is inferior/lateral.
    The lateral corticospinal tract undergoes 90% decussation at the caudal medulla (pyramidal decussation); the remaining ~10% forms the anterior corticospinal tract, which decussates later at spinal cord levels.
    Transection of the lateral corticospinal tract → spastic hemiparesis with a positive Babinski sign.

    Clinical Pearls

    A lesion high in the cervical cord above the brachial plexus cuts off cortical regulation only → spastic upper limb.
    A direct lesion at the level of the brachial plexus (roots C5–T1) cuts off both cortical and local impulses → flaccid upper limb.
    A direct injury to the lumbosacral plexus cuts off all signaling to the lower limb → flaccid.
    Seat-belt fractures damaging the cord above the lumbosacral plexus → spastic lower limbs (intact local plexus fires unregulated).
    Gunshot wounds or direct trauma destroying the lumbosacral plexus itself → always flaccid (the local "generator" is gone).
    A strictly midline blow to the top of the head → possible lower-limb deficits. A lateral blow above the ear → possible upper-limb deficits.
    A lesion in the cerebral cortex (or anywhere above the medulla) produces contralateral sensory/motor deficits, due to decussation.

    🧠 Memory & Mnemonics Recall aids

    "G is for Guwa" (inside): Fasciculus Gracilis = lower limb, most medial (inside). Fasciculus cuneatus = upper limb, lateral.
    Posterior column order: "Sally Loves Thai Cuisine" — Sacral, Lumbar, Thoracic, Cervical, medial → lateral.
    THalamus / THird ventricle: the VPL nucleus sits in the thalamus, which lies lateral to the THird ventricle.
    Pre vs. Post central gyrus: "Pre-motor comes before you move; Post-central comes after the stimulus is sensed." Pre-central = motor (frontal); post-central = sensory (parietal).
    Generator vs. grid: Plexus = home generator (raw power); Cortex = city grid (regulation). Lose the grid only → unregulated power → spastic. Lose the generator → no power → flaccid.
    Homunculus inversion: "Upside-down man" — legs on top/medial, arms and face below/lateral, both at the cortex and in the posterior columns.

    📚 Full Lecture Narrative Complete content

    A complete, English-language narrative reconstruction of both recorded lectures — every explanation, analogy, worked example, and question-and-answer exchange preserved, so nothing from the original teaching is lost.

    Lecture 1 — Spinal Cord Topography and Ascending/Descending Tract Anatomy

    ▶
    Opening — cross-sectional orientation
    The lecturer opens by orienting students to the current slide, confirming they are looking at a presented section of the material and that this is a new section of the topic. He asks how many views of the spinal cord they have — the class answers three — and confirms the current view is the axial cut.
    Gray and white matter organization
    Looking at the spinal cord in axial cuts, the gray matter is found divided into an H-shape, also called the "butterfly" shape, sitting centrally. Laterally lies the white matter. The white matter itself is divided into three parts by the gray matter: the posterior funiculus, located between the two posterior horns; the lateral funiculus, located between the posterior horn and the anterior horn on each side; and the anterior funiculus, located between the two anterior horns. Knowing this division matters because the tractology — the pathways carrying impulses — is concentrated in the lateral funiculus.
    Anterior white commissure
    Another important structure is the anterior white commissure, which connects the two anterior funiculi. It can also be described as lying posterior to the anterior median fissure, or as lying anterior to the horizontal part of the gray matter — that is, anterior to the central canal. It can equally be described as sitting between the two anterior gray horns. This structure matters because most of the ascending pathways do not travel straight up on the same side — a large portion of fibers entering on the left cross to the right, and vice versa, and much of this crossing happens specifically at the anterior white commissure.
    Rexed laminae and Lissauer's tract
    The gray matter itself is subdivided into laminae, from lamina 1 through lamina 10 — called the Rexed laminae, named after the person who first described them. The lecturer points to laminae 5, 6, and 7 on the slide as clinically important units. He notes that a structure equivalent to Rexed lamina 7 exists under a different regional name depending on spinal level — for example, in the lumbar region it carries one name, and in the thoracic region a different name (this becomes the posterior thoracic nucleus/nucleus of Clarke, discussed later with the spinocerebellar tracts). Just lateral to lamina 1 (some texts place it just anterior to lamina 1) lies the posterolateral tract of Lissauer — Lissauer being a German physician.
    Somatotopic organization of the posterior column
    Moving to another cross-sectional cut, the lecturer adds that within the posterior funiculus, the ascending (sensory) fibers are arranged according to a specific order called somatotopical organization: sacral fibers are most medial, then lumbar, then thoracic, then cervical fibers lie most laterally — the arrangement essentially mirrors the vertebral order itself.
    The reversed pattern in other tracts
    He stresses that in most of the other tractology — the other ascending pathways — the somatotopic pattern is the complete opposite: cervical fibers tend to be most medial, and sacral fibers most lateral. The posterior column is the exception. The reason for placing the sacral (lower-limb) fibers most medially in the posterior column specifically: the body places its most vital fibers deepest for protection, and the posterior column is heavily concerned with gait and balance — so lower-limb fibers, being most critical for standing and walking, are tucked most medially. He uses the class's own posture as an example: the fact that everyone is currently sitting upright and balanced is, at that moment, being interpreted through the posterior column pathway.
    Spinocerebellar tracts — location
    Continuing with the ascending pathways, the spinocerebellar tract sits most laterally — specifically, most laterally within the lateral funiculus (recall: the lateral funiculus is the white matter between the posterior and anterior horns). The tract's name reflects its course, from the spine to the cerebellum.
    Spinothalamic tracts — location
    The spinothalamic tract has two divisions, lateral and anterior. The lateral spinothalamic tract sits within the lateral funiculus, but specifically at its medial aspect — that is, medial relative to the lateral-most position occupied by the spinocerebellar tracts. The lecturer emphasizes this distinction so students do not confuse the two: the lateral spinothalamic tract is medial within the lateral funiculus. The anterior spinothalamic tract sits within the anterior funiculus, which he describes as straightforward. The dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts remain most lateral, as already established.
    Descending tracts — overview
    Turning to the descending pathways, the most important is the corticospinal tract, with its two divisions (lateral and anterior). Next is the rubrospinal tract, arising from the red nucleus. Then the tectospinal tract, arising from the tectum — the tectum being the dorsal-most (roof) part of the midbrain, distinct from the tegmentum. The lecturer notes these will be reviewed again on the next slide, since repetition helps retention.
    Posterior column subdivision — gracilis and cuneatus
    Returning to the posterior column, it is divided into two parts by the posterior intermediate sulcus (also called the interfascicular sulcus, or in some descriptions, positioned posterior to the intermediate sulcus): the fasciculus gracilis and the fasciculus cuneatus. To remember which is which, the lecturer offers a mnemonic: gracilis starts with "G," standing for "inside" (medial) — so gracilis is most medial, and cuneatus lies lateral to it.
    Ascending tracts as a general category
    The lecturer summarizes that ascending tracts represent functional pathways carrying sensory information from the periphery to higher levels. Most consist of a chain of three neurons — first-, second-, and third-order. The first-order neuron is always located in the spinal ganglion, which sits lateral to the lateral horn. To reach the spinal ganglion, one is essentially "entering through" the lateral horn region and finding the ganglion there, acting as a relay point. He offers an extended analogy: the first-order neuron is like a station or connection point — comparable to a traveler in Sudan boarding transport from a local market or a land port; all the "passengers" (impulses) converge there before continuing their journey by bus (the axon) onward to the second-order neuron, the next station.
    Decussation as a general rule
    Most of these three-neuron chains have their first-order neuron in the spinal ganglia, and the majority of them decussate before reaching their final destination — crossing from one side to the other. He extends the transport analogy: a traveler heading to Khartoum from this region typically crosses at the Rufa'a bridge before continuing on the eastern road — most of the "buses" (fiber tracts) cross to the opposite side at a specific point along their route, generally from right to left or left to right, with a large share of that crossing occurring at the anterior white commissure.
    Collateral branches and the reflex arc
    These first-order neurons also give rise to collateral branches that serve local spinal reflex arcs — as previously discussed, if something touches you, you withdraw the affected limb immediately, without first thinking about or interpreting what touched you (whether it is a bag or a snake makes no difference to the reflex). This is the spinal reflex arc: sensation enters and motor output is generated at the same spinal level, immediately, without the signal traveling up to the brain first.
    Posterior column–medial lemniscus, function and receptors
    The posterior column is also called the posterior column–medial lemniscus pathway, named for its continuing route (the medial lemniscus). It mediates fine touch, conscious proprioception, and vibratory sense. Regarding proprioception, the lecturer notes there are two types — conscious and unconscious — since the term "conscious" implies a corresponding "unconscious" type exists elsewhere. The pathway is somatotopically organized, as already discussed (sacral most medial). It receives input from Pacinian and Meissner corpuscles, joint receptors, muscle spindles, and Golgi tendon organs — logical, since it relates to position sense, which draws on tendons, muscles, and joints.
    First-order neuron location, and limb-level somatotopy
    The first-order neuron, as established, is found at every spinal level. Its axons continue as the fasciculus gracilis (from the lower extremity) and the fasciculus cuneatus (from the upper extremity). Reframing the earlier sacral/lumbar/thoracic/cervical ordering into a simpler two-part split: the upper limb corresponds to the lateral portion, and the lower limb to the medial portion.
    Second-order neuron and the medial lemniscus
    These fibers ascend in the posterior columns and terminate in the gracile and cuneate nuclei of the medulla — the axon "goes home" to its correspondingly-named nucleus, just as (in the lecturer's example) Ahmed goes to Ahmed's house and Fatima goes to Fatima's house: fasciculus gracilis goes to the nucleus gracilis, fasciculus cuneatus goes to the nucleus cuneatus, both located in the medulla oblongata. This is the second-order neuron — continuing the earlier travel analogy, if the first-order neuron is the starting point, the second-order neuron is the next stop along the journey. The second-order neuron gives rise to axons that decussate as the internal arcuate fibers — this is the structure that performs the crossing — forming a compact fiber bundle on the opposite side renamed the medial lemniscus. The medial lemniscus ascends through the contralateral brainstem to terminate in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus.
    Third-order neuron and the postcentral gyrus
    From the thalamus, the third-order neuron projects via the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus, the primary sensory area. The lecturer reviews the relevant landmarks: the central sulcus separates the frontal lobe (anterior) from the parietal lobe (posterior). Gyri immediately adjacent to the central sulcus are named for their position relative to it — the precentral gyrus, in the frontal lobe, and the postcentral gyrus, in the parietal lobe. The frontal lobe (precentral gyrus) governs motor function; the parietal lobe (postcentral gyrus) governs sensory function.
    Walking the pathway through a diagram
    Using a diagram, the lecturer retraces the entire route: sensation from Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles enters the dorsal root ganglion, then travels into the posterior funiculus (as opposed to the lateral or anterior funiculus, since the name "posterior column" tells you where it goes). Within the posterior funiculus, lower-limb fibers sit medially. The medial fibers form the fasciculus gracilis, the lateral fibers the fasciculus cuneatus; both terminate in the medulla oblongata, in the correspondingly named nuclei — the medial one in the nucleus gracilis, the lateral one in the nucleus cuneatus. From there, decussation occurs — shown on the diagram just anterior to the central canal — via the compact internal arcuate fibers, renamed the medial lemniscus on the contralateral side. The medial lemniscus continues through the rest of the medulla, through the pons, and through the midbrain, arriving at the thalamus (identified on the diagram as sitting lateral to the third ventricle). From the thalamus, the pathway proceeds directly to the postcentral gyrus.
    Cortical (homunculus) organization is inverted
    The postcentral gyrus itself has an internal organization: the lower limb is represented medially and superiorly in the brain, while the upper limb is represented laterally and inferiorly. Combined with the earlier rule that the right hemisphere controls the left side of the body and vice versa, this creates a fully inverted map. The lecturer offers a memorable clinical example: if someone strikes another person with a stick on the very top-middle of the head, expect the legs to be affected, since lower-limb representation sits superiorly. If instead struck laterally, just above the ear, the upper limb would be affected instead, since upper-limb representation sits inferiorly and laterally there. He also identifies the lateral sulcus, which separates the frontal and parietal lobes above from the temporal lobe below.
    Second full walkthrough — consolidating the pathway
    The lecturer walks through the pathway once more from the beginning, checking understanding at each step: sensation begins at the Pacinian/Meissner corpuscles, tendons, muscles, and joints; travels to the first-order neuron in the dorsal root ganglion; enters the posterior funiculus of the spinal cord. Fibers are organized with sacral most medial, then lumbar, then thoracic, then cervical most lateral — or, grouped more broadly, lumbosacral fibers (lower limb) are most medial and cervical/upper-thoracic fibers (upper limb) are most lateral. These fibers ascend the posterior funiculus of the spinal cord to the lower part of the medulla oblongata, arriving at the gracile and cuneate nuclei — this is the relay to the second-order neuron. The second-order neuron crosses to the contralateral side (so a signal entering on the right ends up on the left), via what is specifically named, at this location, the internal arcuate fiber; after crossing, the bundle is renamed the medial lemniscus. The medial lemniscus continues through the medulla, pons, and midbrain until reaching the thalamus, where it relays at the VPL. From the VPL, the pathway continues through the internal capsule — specifically the posterior limb — described as resembling a hand shape, with an anterior limb and a posterior limb joined at a bend called the genu. The pathway travels through the posterior limb to reach its final destination: the postcentral gyrus, located in the parietal lobe. The upper limb representation sits inferiorly, and the lower limb representation sits superiorly (most medially) — restated once more via the same stick-injury example: a blow to the very top of the head affects the legs; a blow above the ear affects the arms.

    Lecture 2 — Clinical Application: Spastic vs. Flaccid Limbs

    ▶
    Opening question
    The lecturer opens by asking the class: who becomes flaccid and who becomes spastic, and under what circumstances — that is, who ends up limp/relaxed versus tense/rigid, and why. After a pause for responses, he begins the explanation.
    Two sources of impulse — the plexus and the cortex
    Simply put: the brachial plexus and the lumbosacral plexus each generate outgoing impulses to their respective region — the lumbosacral plexus to the lower limb, and the brachial plexus to the upper limb. These plexuses generate their own signal independently. However, that signal is normally regulated and refined by descending input from the cortex, which smooths the raw plexus signal into a fine, controlled movement.
    Worked example — high cervical injury
    Consider a patient injured in an accident, struck high in the neck. The impulses reaching the hand — are they coming from the cortex and the brachial plexus together, or from the brachial plexus alone? In this case, from the brachial plexus alone, since the cortical connection above has been severed. That means the signal arrives strong and unregulated — which is why the result is spasticity.
    Worked example — direct brachial plexus injury
    Now take the same type of patient, but this time injured directly at the level where the brachial plexus arises — the vertebral levels from C5 to T1. The impulses to the upper limb — where would they now come from? Nowhere. Both the ascending output from the plexus and the descending input from above have been lost. As a result, the upper limb becomes flaccid.
    Same logic applied to the lower limb
    The lecturer checks understanding, then applies the identical logic to the lower limb and the lumbosacral plexus. The lower limb normally receives impulses from both the lumbosacral plexus and the cortex. If one of the two is cut — for example, a person injured in a seat-belt-related accident, where the fracture occurs above the level of the lumbosacral plexus — all impulses arriving from above are lost, but the impulses generated by the lumbosacral plexus itself remain active. Would those remaining impulses be strong or weak? Strong — so the lower limb becomes spastic.
    Worked example — direct lumbosacral plexus injury (gunshot)
    Next, consider a different patient with a gunshot wound striking directly at the level of the lumbosacral plexus. The impulses reaching the leg now come from nowhere — both the plexus's own output and the "general power supply" from above have been cut. The lecturer extends the earlier generator analogy explicitly here: you might have a home generator as well as a connection to the general city power supply. If only the city supply is cut, the home generator — which normally runs at a higher, unregulated level before being smoothed by the city supply's regulation — continues running on its own, producing a stronger, unregulated output. But if the injury instead damages the internal wiring of the house itself, you lose both sources entirely — neither the generator's own output nor the general supply reaches the target.
    Closing remarks and forward references
    The lecturer reassures the class that this material will be revisited and reinforced in later sessions — repetition is intentional. He notes that by this point students already have a working knowledge of the gray and white matter divisions of the spinal cord. He adds a few final descriptive facts: the spinal cord is roughly 1 cm in width, roughly 30 g in weight — about 2% of the weight of the brain — and briefly mentions the meninges as the next topic. He previews that the thalamus lecture will revisit the VPL and the intralaminar nuclei (already introduced here), and that the brainstem lectures will build on the medial lemniscus, crus cerebri, tectum, tegmentum, the pyramids of the medulla oblongata, and the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles — all already encountered in this lecture. He closes by encouraging the class to keep up with reading from the start, reassuring them that any gap can be caught up on, and that the material forms a continuous, connected cycle rather than isolated facts.
